title: Follow that man
hookLine: Zeno asks the bookseller where men like Socrates can be found, and Crates the Cynic walks past
carry: nothing terrible has happened to you
last: ZENO'S SHIPWRECK — I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.

lines: ZENO LOOKS UP FROM THE PAGE.
WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THIS?
cards: Zeno looks up from the page. Socrates has been dead for generations, so he asks the bookseller: where can I find men like this? Real ones.
Alive. And right then, as if the story had been waiting for its cue, a strange figure walks past the shop door. The bookseller points at him and says three words.

teach.b: The man walking past was Crates, a Cynic philosopher. The Cynics were the punk rockers of ancient Greece. They owned almost nothing, slept in public, said exactly what they thought, and mocked anything fake.
The name comes from the Greek for dog-like, because they lived as openly as dogs. Crates had been born rich, in Thebes, and given his wealth away.
Ancient writers say people called him the door-opener, because he walked into any house he liked and gave the family advice, and they were glad to see him.

A woman named Hipparchia, from a wealthy family, fell in love with him, chose his life of the road over her comfortable one, and became a philosopher in her own right. So Zeno followed, and became Crates's student.
But Zeno was shy, and the Cynics were shameless on purpose. Diogenes Laërtius tells this story.
Crates hands Zeno a pot of lentil soup and tells him to carry it through a busy part of Athens. Zeno, embarrassed, tries to hide it under his cloak. Crates cracks the pot with his staff.
Soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno runs. And Crates calls after him, roughly: why are you running, my little Phoenician?
Nothing terrible has happened to you.
Embarrassment, Crates was saying, isn't harm. And look at how it all began. A curious question, asked out loud.
And the nerve to get up from a bookseller's bench and follow him out the door.

how: In the ancient schools, people learned philosophy by attaching themselves to a living teacher and following them about; many people today still seek out a teacher or a community to learn from in person.

o: a Greek Cynic who gave away his wealth to live simply
a Greek general who led armies as far as India
a Greek sculptor who carved statues of the gods

games.q: the bookshop and the Cynic — tap the pairs.
p: points and says: follow that man
chose the Cynic life and philosophy

s: the word Cynic comes from the Greek for dog-like
they lived as openly as dogs, and were proud of it.
he was born rich, in Thebes, and gave his wealth away.
Zeno was comfortable with the Cynics' shamelessness from the start
he was shy. Crates broke a pot of soup on him to make the point.

games.q: you're Crates. your shy new student is hiding a pot of lentil soup under his cloak as you cross a crowded street. what do you do?
o: let him hide it. he'll learn in time.
crack the pot with your staff.
take the pot and carry it yourself.
games.why: Crates breaks the pot, the soup runs down Zeno's legs, Zeno runs, and Crates calls: nothing terrible has happened to you.

practice: Sit, and let the breath settle, then ask Zeno's question in your own words: where can I find more of this? Let one curiosity come, a subject, a skill, a kind of person you'd like to learn from.
Then picture the bookseller pointing, and notice where the finger goes: a book, a class, a person you could ask.

wordCard.voice: Crates. The Cynic who walked past a bookshop, and the man a shipwrecked merchant got up to follow.

orig.note: Greek, kynikos: dog-like, from kyon, dog. The name of the Cynic philosophers, and the root of English cynic.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing terrible has happened to you. Spilled soup is only spilled soup. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.2–3 (the bookshop; the lentil soup)
